# The Fast Path {#sec-fast-path}

```{python}
#| label: fast-setup
# The evaluation project's results, computed by its own script (scripts/evaluation.py), and
# the starter repository readers copy.
from scripts import evaluation as ev
from scripts.prose import number_words, text_holds

S = ev.summary()
best = S["best_version"]
versions = [r["version"] for r in S["releases"]]
WORD = number_words()
QUOTED_WORD = number_words(lang="en")  # inside the Acme report's own English sentence
starter = ev.files(ev.STARTER)
n_tests = sum(1 for f in starter if f.startswith("tests/test_"))
text_holds(not any(f.endswith(".qmd") or f == "AGENTS.md" for f in starter),
           "the starter has no Quarto file and no AGENTS.md")
text_holds("notebooks/explore.ipynb" in starter, "the starter's notebook")
# Every prompt in this chapter was dry-run, verbatim, by Claude Code (Opus 5.5) in a fresh
# copy of starters/eval-repo on 2026-11-18: all four worked, the three formats showed the same
# numbers, and a fresh clone rebuilt them; the pitfalls below are what that run met.
```

You already use a terminal and Git, and you have a repository full of work that ends up,
one way or another, in documents: a notebook, a script that writes a results file, a test
suite. This chapter adds Quarto to such a repository and takes it, in under an hour, to a
report in HTML, Word and PDF whose every number is computed from the repository's own
results, with a guard that stops the build when a sentence stops being true, reviewed as a
pull request. It is written for analysts, data scientists, ML and research engineers and
technical founders. If the terminal or Git is new to you, take the other route, Chapters 4
and 5 (@sec-setup and @sec-first-report), and come back to this chapter afterwards: it
assumes what they teach.

The repository is a small, realistic one: Acme Signals, a fictional two-person start-up,
evaluates the releases of a model that ranks a bank's marketing contacts by how likely each
is to subscribe, on real public data. Part III builds the rest of its publications from the
same results. Every step works the same on a repository of your own, and the last section
says what to change.

::: opener
- Add Quarto to an existing repository without changing how its code runs.
- Render an existing notebook, and say what `--execute` does to it.
- Ask for a report in three formats that computes every number from the repository's
  results, and check it as its reader would.
- Guard a sentence whose wording depends on the results, and review the change as a pull
  request and a fresh clone.

Start from
: Git and a terminal you are at home in, one coding agent (@sec-assistant), and the workshop's
  repository cloned to `~/quarto-workshop`.

You build
: `~/acme-eval`: the repository with `AGENTS.md`, a report in HTML, Word and PDF, a guard,
  and a branch reviewed as a pull request.

Checkpoint
: `checkpoints/14-eval-start/`
:::

## Is this your route? {#sec-fast-route}

Take the fast path if all of these are routine for you: moving between folders and reading
an error in a terminal; `git status`, `git diff`, branches and commits; installing a
command-line tool. Then you need four tools at the versions below, and an agent.

| Tool | Check | Needed |
|---|---|---|
| Git | `git --version` | any recent version |
| uv | `uv --version` | manages each project's Python and packages (@sec-environments) |
| Quarto | `quarto --version` | 1.10 or newer |
| GitHub CLI | `gh auth status` | signed in, for the pull request |

: What the fast path needs. {#tbl-fast-tools}

If one is missing, the agent installs it with the prompt in @sec-step-tools, and
@sec-step-assistant installs the agent itself. Then clone the workshop's repository, which
holds the starter, if you have not:

```bash
git clone https://github.com/project-delphi/quarto-workshop.git ~/quarto-workshop
```

## The repository {#sec-fast-repo}

Copy the starter and make it a repository of your own, with one commit, as if you had
cloned it from your team. In the terminal:

::: {.you}
```bash
cp -R ~/quarto-workshop/starters/eval-repo ~/acme-eval
cd ~/acme-eval
git init -b main
git add .
git commit -m "Evaluation repo, as copied"
```
:::

It is a Python project like many in practice, `{python} WORD[len(starter)]` files and no
Quarto in sight:

| Path | Holds |
|---|---|
| `data/` | the UCI Bank Marketing table, real and unchanged, with its README and licence; a small file of business figures marked SYNTHETIC |
| `releases.yml` | the `{python} WORD[len(versions)]` releases of the model, `{python} ", ".join(versions)` |
| `src/acme_eval/` | loading, the models and the metrics, as a package |
| `scripts/evaluate.py` | fits each release once and writes every result to `outputs/` |
| `tests/` | `{python} WORD[n_tests]` pytest files: the data's checksum, no leakage, metrics, outputs |
| `notebooks/explore.ipynb` | an exploratory notebook, saved without outputs |
| `pyproject.toml`, `uv.lock` | the environment, pinned |

: The starter repository. {#tbl-fast-starter}

Run its own checks once, as you would on a colleague's branch, so that you know the baseline:

::: {.you}
```bash
uv run python scripts/evaluate.py
uv run pytest -q
```
:::

The first command builds `.venv/` from `uv.lock`, fits the releases and writes `outputs/`;
the second runs the tests. Neither knows anything about documents, and nothing in this
chapter changes how they run. That is the design to keep: **one script computes the results
once; every document reads them.** The documents can then be rebuilt, reformatted and
reviewed without ever re-fitting a model, and a reviewer can trust that the report and the
model card quote the same run.

## Rules before requests {#sec-fast-rules}

Start the agent in the repository (`claude`, `codex` or `agy`) and give it the project's
rules before any work. The prompt names what a rule file holds (@sec-agents-md), and asks
the agent to read the code first, so that the rules fit this repository rather than a
generic one:

::: {.prompt}
```default
Read README.md, pyproject.toml, scripts/evaluate.py and tests/, then write AGENTS.md for this repository: its scope (say the company is fictional); rules (data/ is read-only; documents read outputs/ and never fit a model; every number in a document comes from outputs/ through code, never typed; run python, pytest and quarto through `uv run`; never commit outputs/ or rendered files); and the commands to evaluate, test and render. Show me the file.
```
:::

::: {.agent}
reads the four sources · writes `AGENTS.md`
:::

Read what it wrote. Each rule should be one you could check by reading a diff: "documents
never fit a model" is checkable, "keep the code clean" is not. Then start a branch for the
work, as you would for any change you mean to review, and commit the rules on it. In a second
terminal tab:

::: {.you}
```bash
git switch -c add-report
git add AGENTS.md
git commit -m "Write the project's rules for agents"
```
:::

## A notebook you already have {#sec-fast-notebook}

Most repositories already hold notebooks. Quarto renders a `.ipynb` file directly, to any of
its formats, so a notebook can be published before anything is rewritten.

::: {.prompt}
```default
Run `uv add ipykernel nbclient nbformat`, then render notebooks/explore.ipynb to HTML with `uv run quarto render notebooks/explore.ipynb --execute`. Tell me where the HTML went and what `git status` shows.
```
:::

::: {.agent}
`uv add …` · `uv run quarto render notebooks/explore.ipynb --execute`
:::

The three packages are what Quarto needs to run Python code: a kernel, and the libraries
that drive a notebook. `--execute` matters. A notebook is rendered **as it was saved**:
without the flag, Quarto shows the outputs stored in the file, or none, and runs nothing.
With it, Quarto runs every cell first, and, as the vocabulary to know, *writes the new
outputs back into the notebook*.

::: think
After the render, `git status` lists `notebooks/explore.ipynb` as modified, as well as
`pyproject.toml` and `uv.lock`. You did not ask for the notebook to change. What happened,
and what do you do?

`--execute` saved the outputs it computed into the notebook: in the test run, several
hundred changed lines. Whether to keep them is a team's decision, so make it on purpose.
This repository keeps its notebooks without outputs, so undo that change and commit only the
two files that record the new packages.
:::

::: {.you}
```bash
git restore notebooks/explore.ipynb
git add pyproject.toml uv.lock
git commit -m "Add the packages Quarto needs to run Python"
```
:::

The HTML went beside the notebook, `notebooks/explore.html`, with a folder of its files;
`.gitignore` leaves both out.

A notebook can also become a Quarto document: `quarto convert notebooks/explore.ipynb`
writes `explore.qmd`, plain text that diffs and reviews line by line, and that executes every
time it renders. Convert a notebook when it is turning into a document that others read; keep
it a notebook while it is a place for exploring.

## A report that reads the results {#sec-fast-report}

Now the deliverable: a report of the evaluation for the people who decide which release to
ship. Its headline metric is *ROC AUC*, the probability that a release ranks a random
subscriber above a random non-subscriber: 0.5 is a random ranking, 1 a perfect one. It is a new `.qmd` file beside the code, and it is the specification, in one prompt, of
everything the report must do and how you will check it:

::: {.prompt}
```default
Run `uv run python scripts/evaluate.py`. Create report.qmd (formats html, docx and typst; hide code) that reads only outputs/: a sentence naming the best version by ROC AUC with its AUC and 95% interval as inline code; a table of every version's metrics, labelled `tbl-metrics`, with a caption and referred to in the text; and the ROC curves as a figure labelled `fig-roc`, with a caption and alt text. Render all three formats and tell me the AUC each one shows.
```
:::

::: {.agent}
`uv run python scripts/evaluate.py` · writes `report.qmd` · `uv run quarto render report.qmd` → `report.html`, `report.docx`, `report.pdf`
:::

Every phrase of the prompt is vocabulary that maps to one feature, which is why it can be
short:

| The prompt says | Quarto's feature | You check |
|---|---|---|
| formats html, docx and typst | three formats from one file (@sec-formats); Typst makes the PDF | three files, each opened |
| hide code | `echo: false` | no code in any output |
| inline code | `` `{{python}} …` `` in a sentence (@sec-code-cells) | the sentence's number equals `outputs/` |
| labelled `tbl-metrics`, referred to | a cross-reference: `@tbl-metrics` becomes "Table 1", a link | the text says "Table 1", not "??" |
| caption and alt text | `tbl-cap`, `fig-cap`, `fig-alt` (@sec-cell-options) | the caption says what it is; the alt text, what it shows |
| reads only outputs/ | the project's rule, from `AGENTS.md` | the diff: no `fit`, no model code |

: The report prompt, phrase by phrase. {#tbl-fast-vocab}

Then verify it three ways (@sec-three-skills). **Read the diff**: `git status` should list
`report.qmd` as new and nothing else changed, and the file should read files from `outputs/`
and fit nothing. **Inspect the render**: open `report.html`, `report.docx` and `report.pdf`.
The render prints `Output created` for the first format only, so look for all three files.
In the finished project the sentence reads:

> Of the `{python} QUOTED_WORD[len(versions)]` releases, **`{python} best`** ranks best: its ROC AUC on the
> `{python} f"{S['test_rows']:,}"` held-out contacts is
> `{python} ev.interval(best, "roc_auc")`.

**Compare it with the source**, without the report: `grep roc_auc outputs/metrics.csv`
prints each version's value with its `low` and `high`, and the report's three formats must
all agree with it.

::: pitfall
Word does not get the alt text. In the test runs, Quarto 1.10.20 put the figure's file name,
or nothing, in the Word picture's description, never `fig-alt`; the HTML had it. If a reader
of the Word file uses a screen reader, add the description in Word, and check each format a
reader will use.
:::

## A guard for the sentence {#sec-fast-guard}

The report's first sentence names a winner. Inline code keeps its numbers current, but the
*word* "best", and the name beside it, are only true while the data say so. A *guard* is a
line of code beside such a sentence that stops the render if it becomes false
(@sec-water-website). It is ordinary Python, so it fits the repository's own package:

::: {.prompt}
```default
Add src/acme_eval/claims.py with `claim(condition, sentence)`, which raises an error quoting the sentence when the condition is false. In report.qmd, guard the sentence that names the best version with it, and add a rule to AGENTS.md: a sentence whose wording depends on the results gets a claim. Prove the guard works: render once with a deliberately wrong version name, show me the error, then restore the right one and render again.
```
:::

The proof is the point. A guard you have never seen fail is a guard you have not tested, and
the prompt makes the agent break it on purpose and show you the message. For it to be able
to fail, the sentence's version must be written somewhere a person could get it wrong, and
checked against `outputs/`: a name read straight from the results could never disagree with
them. Agents word the message differently; in the finished project it reads:

```text
ClaimError: The results no longer support this sentence: The best version named in this
report has the highest ROC AUC in metrics.csv.
```

Check afterwards that the deliberate mistake is gone. A failed render leaves the previous
`report.html`, `.docx` and `.pdf` where they were, so an old file can look like a success:
read the render's last lines, and the sentence in the source. Then commit:

::: {.you}
```bash
git status
git add -A
git commit -m "Add a report that reads outputs/, with a guard"
```
:::

`.gitignore` already leaves out `outputs/`, `.venv/` and the rendered files, so `git add -A`
takes only sources: `AGENTS.md`'s new rule, `report.qmd` and `claims.py`. Read `git status`
first anyway: in the test run, a notebook full of outputs went into this commit because the
restore above was skipped, and `git status` was where it showed.

::: catchup
```default
Catch me up: follow ../quarto-workshop/checkpoints/14-eval-start/README.md
```
:::

## Review it as a pull request {#sec-fast-pr}

A change an agent made is reviewed like a colleague's: on a branch, as a pull request, with
the diff read file by file before it reaches `main` (@sec-git). Put the repository on GitHub,
private, and open the pull request. In the terminal:

::: {.you}
```bash
git switch main
gh repo create acme-eval --private --source=. --push
git switch add-report
git push -u origin add-report
gh pr create --base main --fill
```
:::

`gh repo create … --source=. --push` creates the repository from this folder and pushes
`main`; `git push -u` pushes the branch; `gh pr create --fill` opens a pull request titled
and described from its commits, and prints its address. On the pull request's *Files changed*
tab, or with `gh pr diff` in the terminal, review it as you would any other:

| Check | Asks | Here |
|---|---|---|
| Scope | Did only the files I meant change? | `AGENTS.md`, `report.qmd`, `claims.py`, `pyproject.toml`, `uv.lock`; nothing in `data/`, `tests/` or `notebooks/` |
| Correctness | Does a number match its source? | the report's AUC against `outputs/metrics.csv` |
| Rebuild | Does what was committed build on its own? | a fresh clone renders the same report (below) |

: The three checks of @tbl-three-checks, applied to a pull request. {#tbl-fast-review}

The last check is the one a reviewer cannot do by reading. Clone the repository afresh and
build it from nothing; the results come first, because `outputs/` is computed, not
committed:

::: {.you}
```bash
git clone ~/acme-eval /tmp/acme-check
cd /tmp/acme-check
git switch add-report
uv run python scripts/evaluate.py
uv run quarto render report.qmd
```
:::

The clone's `report.html` must show the same `{python} f"{ev.value(best, 'roc_auc')['value']:.3f}"`.
A render before the evaluation stops with `FileNotFoundError` for `outputs/summary.json`:
that is the clone telling you, correctly, that results are computed, not stored. If anything
else fails, something the report needs lives only in your folder: commit it and clone again.
When the clone agrees, merge the pull request. A build service can run the same fresh-clone
check on every pull request, so that nobody has to remember it.

## On your own repository {#sec-fast-own}

Everything above transfers. Point the prompts at your own files:

- **Rules.** Name your results folder (`outputs/`, `results/`, `reports/data/`) and your
  commands in `AGENTS.md`. If your code computes results inside notebooks, the first job is a
  script that writes them to files: documents that re-run an analysis are slow and can
  disagree with each other.
- **Dependencies.** `ipykernel`, `nbclient` and `nbformat` join your environment, through
  uv, Poetry, pip or conda, as your project manages it; Quarto itself is a separate program
  and adds no Python dependency.
- **Ignore the outputs.** Add the rendered files and the results folder to `.gitignore`.
- **Where the report lives.** At the top of the repository, or in `reports/`; one `.qmd` file
  needs no `_quarto.yml`. A folder of several documents becomes a Quarto *project*
  (@sec-london-website).

::: tryit
Run the four prompts and the pull request on the starter, or on your own repository.

::: done
the pull request shows the rules, the report and the guard, its three formats agree with
`outputs/metrics.csv`, and a fresh clone renders the same report.
:::
:::

## Summary {.unnumbered}

::: keyideas
- Quarto joins an existing repository as one `.qmd` file and three Python packages; how the
  code runs does not change.
- Compute results once, in a script, into files; every document reads the files and fits
  nothing.
- A notebook renders as saved; `--execute` runs it and writes the outputs back into it.
- A prompt made of named features ("inline code", "labelled `tbl-metrics`", "alt text") gets
  those features, and each comes with a check.
- Guard the sentences whose words depend on the results, and watch each guard fail once.
- Review the change as a pull request, and rebuild it from a fresh clone.
:::

The report is the first of the project's publications. Part III builds the rest from the same
results: a model card, a stakeholder deck, a project site with one brand, and a white paper.
If you came by the fast path, Part II's London guide is there for reference when a chapter
points to it.
